links.comparator_used: RAG over general Google internet search results (open web search)
links.outcome: Hallucination rate (medically harmful or misinformation) rated by 2 clinicians
links.effect: CIS-based chatbots 0% (GPT-4) and 6% (GPT-3.5) vs Google-based 6% and 10%; for questions not covered by CIS, Google-based chatbots 19% (GPT-4) and 35% (GPT-3.5); Google vs CIS OR 9.4 (95% CI 1.2-17.5, P<.01)
links.tradeoff: CIS chatbots declined to answer questions not covered by CIS content, whereas Google chatbots responded in 52% (GPT-4) and 71% (GPT-3.5) of those cases; overall response rates for RAG chatbots fell (36% to 81%).
links.quote: Using reference data from Google searches generated more hallucinations than using CIS data, with an OR of 9.4 (95% CI 1.2-17.5, P<.01); the OR for the conventional chatbot was 16.1 (95% CI 3.7-50.0, P<.001).

links.comparator_used: Conventional chatbots with no reference information (LLM training knowledge alone)
links.outcome: Hallucination rate of GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 chatbots
links.effect: Conventional chatbots about 40% hallucination vs CIS-RAG 0% (GPT-4) and 6% (GPT-3.5) and Google-RAG 6% (GPT-4) and 10% (GPT-3.5); conventional vs CIS OR 16.1 (95% CI 3.7-50.0, P<.001)
links.tradeoff: Conventional chatbots answered every question, but RAG chatbots sometimes declined to answer when information was lacking, with response rate falling to 36%-81%.
links.quote: Using RAG with reliable information sources significantly reduces the hallucination rate of generative AI chatbots and increases the ability to admit lack of information, making them more suitable for general use, where users need to be provided with accurate information.
